pages.text: Edinam wrote a letter to his cousin Wunpini. “It rained all night here. Our yard is wet, and the plants are green. What is the weather like where you live?” He posted the letter and waited.
sentences: Edinam wrote a letter to his cousin Wunpini.
“It rained all night here.
Our yard is wet, and the plants are green.
What is the weather like where you live?” He posted the letter and waited.
pages.alt: Edinam sitting at a desk beside an open window looking out onto lush rain-washed green banana leaves and wet courtyard earth as he writes a letter.

pages.text: Wunpini wrote back. “Here it is dry. The grass is dry and yellow, and the wind is dusty. But when the rains come, farmers plant their seeds, and the fields turn green.” She sent a picture of a dry field and a green field.
sentences: Wunpini wrote back.

pages.alt: In northern Ghana, Wunpini sits at a wooden table holding two colourful crayon drawings side by side: one golden dry savanna field and one lush green farm.

pages.text: Their teacher explained, “Many parts of Ghana have two main seasons: a wet season and a dry season. The seasons come again and again every year. We call this a recurring event.”
sentences: Their teacher explained, “Many parts of Ghana have two main seasons: a wet season and a dry season.
The seasons come again and again every year.
We call this a recurring event.”
pages.alt: In a bright classroom, the teacher points to two large wordless paintings on the board—one showing rain clouds over green crops and one showing bright sun over golden grass.

pages.text: “But the months are not the same everywhere,” said the teacher. “In some parts of the country, the rains come in two periods. In others, they come once. So we ask local elders and farmers, and we read the weather reports.”
sentences: “But the months are not the same everywhere,” said the teacher.

pages.alt: The teacher standing beside a simple unlabelled silhouette map of Ghana showing green southern forest and golden northern savanna while pupils listen.

pages.text: Edinam and Wunpini made a list. In the wet season, plants grow fast, clothes dry slowly and children carry umbrellas. In the dry season, the air is dry, the dust rises, and we drink more water and look after our skin.

pages.alt: Split scene: on the left Edinam walks under a bright umbrella past lush green bushes; on the right Wunpini drinks water from a cup in sunny dry breeze.

pages.text: At the end of the term, the cousins swapped drawings. “Seasons come and go,” wrote Wunpini. “Each one has a job,” wrote Edinam. “The wet one feeds the plants, and the dry one lets the harvest dry.” They looked forward to their next letters.
